title: Understanding the Emergence of Seemingly Useless Features in Next-Token Predictors
claim: A training gradient splits into direct, pre-cached and shared components, each contributing separately to improving a feature.
layout: 2 panels: Transformer information-flow diagram left, gradient vector decomposition right
description: Two panels. The left panel is a Transformer computation graph. Four token columns (you, need, is, love at the top; all, you, need, is at the bottom) are connected through layers k=0, 1 and 2, drawn as dashed cyan horizontal lines. Gray rounded boxes mark the blocks. Faint orange lines show the shared attention paths. Bold green and blue paths trace the direct and pre-cached routes through position i=2 and layer k=1. A turquoise rectangle marks the residual stream node there. The right panel is a vector diagram. From the point θ_t, orange (shared), green (direct) and blue (pre-cached) arrows add up to a black full-gradient arrow. Dashed projections onto a horizontal axis give I_pre-cached, I_shared and I_direct. The sum is the decrease in feature mismatch. The eye goes first to the colored paths in the left panel.
caption: Left: An illustration of the information-flow decomposition for i = 2 and k = 1 into direct, pre-cached, and shared components. Direct and pre-cached paths must pass through the residual stream at position i = 2 and layer k = 1; any other path is considered shared. The turquoise rectangle indicates rk=1
abstract: Trained Transformers have been shown to compute abstract features that appear redundant for predicting the immediate next token. We identify which components of the gradient signal from the next-token prediction objective give rise to this phenomenon, and we propose a method to estimate the influence of those components on the emergence of specific features. After validating our approach on toy tasks, we use it to interpret the origins of the world model in OthelloGPT and syntactic features in a small language model. Finally, we apply our framework to a pretrained LLM, showing that features with extremely high or low influence on future tokens tend to be related to formal reasoning domains such as code. Overall, our work takes a step toward understanding hidden features of Transformers through the lens of their development during training.
